clue.text: Slur sees liberal undone after having got elected

indicators.note: Liberal means loose rather than political here, and letters treated loosely do not stay in the order they were handed over in.
After sends the piece in front of it to the back, so the shuffled letters finish the entry rather than start it.

blocks.note: a candidate who wins the seat is in
six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician wrecked by gossip not long after winning the seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' offers itself as the party the politician belongs to and only means loose. The word it loosens is standing right next to it, and 'sees' is joinery with nothing inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An innuendo is a sly insinuation about somebody's character, which is the aspersion a slur casts rather than a smudging of sound.

clue.text: See 25
Daredevil bats taking cover

blocks.note: bats is British slang for crazy, the same idea as batty
a cap is the cover that goes on a bottle or a pen

explanation.surface: A fearless batsman keeping his head down at the crease.
explanation.walkthrough: Both wordplay words are hiding inside a cricket picture: 'bats' as a verb and 'cover' as the fielding position square of the wicket. Neither is doing that job in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A madcap is a reckless, impulsive person, which is what anyone called a daredevil is.

clue.text: Dumber pants, a forerunner of shorts?

indicators.note: Pants is British slang for rubbish, and letters called rubbish have been thrown out of their proper order.

blocks.note: six letters of the fodder
the article joins the fodder as its seventh letter

explanation.surface: A sillier pair of trousers that fashion wore before it got round to shorts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' has to be read as the insult meaning rubbish, not as the garment the surface is dressed in. The definition names a word by what stands in front of it in a phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Bermuda shorts, the knee-length pair named after the mid-Atlantic island, put that island's name directly in front of the word shorts.

clue.text: In respect of failing to start a Latin exam

indicators.note: A word that fails to start never gets its opening letter down, so it is written from the second letter on.

blocks.note: for does this job in phrases like 'for my part'
the article taken at face value
l is the dictionary's short form for Latin

explanation.surface: A note about a candidate who never turned up for the Latin paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In respect of' reads as the opening of a formal letter and is really a three-letter word waiting to be docked. The exam meant is the spoken kind, which nothing in the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral is the spoken examination set in a language course, so 'exam' names it plainly.

clue.text: ‘Green’s getting stony!’ – a familiar complaint

blocks.note: a village green is a common, the patch of open land an English village is built around
a stony look or a stony silence is an unfeeling one

explanation.surface: A grumble that somebody named Green has turned mean with money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' is the pivot: a grumble in the surface, an ailment in the definition. 'Green' wears a capital to look like a surname, and the open land it really names sits at the centre of an English village.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint is the old word for an illness, and this is the one everybody catches every winter, so the phrase names the most ordinary ailment there is.

clue.text: Wine component almost turning brown!

indicators.note: Almost a word is the word one letter short, so the final letter never arrives.

blocks.note: skin turning brown in the sun is tanning

explanation.surface: A drop of wine on the point of going brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' is the trap: in a down clue it offers itself as an instruction to write letters upwards, and it is only half of an ordinary phrase about sunbathing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tannins are the compounds drawn from grape skins and stalks that give a red wine its dry, mouth-puckering grip.

clue.text: Rather personal hint

blocks.note: the adjective for what is close, private and not for general sharing
the verb for letting something be known without ever saying it outright

explanation.surface: A suggestion that strays into private territory.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words, two definitions and no joinery at all, which is why the clue looks too short to be doing anything. The second definition is a verb although the sentence parks it as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Something intimate is closely personal; and to intimate is to convey a thing indirectly, which is what a hint does.

clue.text: Wine jar adapted to store a frigid body

indicators.note: Something adapted has been altered to fit a new purpose, and letters altered that way come out in a different order.
To store something is to put it away inside something else, so the letters named next go within the ones just made.

blocks.note: three letters rearranged, leaving a gap after the first
Io is one of Jupiter's moons, a body out in the cold of the outer solar system

explanation.surface: A jar reworked to hold something freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body' offers a corpse and supplies a moon instead — astronomers call anything in orbit a body, which is what makes the two letters fair. The container is only three letters wide, so the gap has to be made by shuffling first.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioja is the red made in the Rioja region of northern Spain, so 'wine' names it by its class.

clue.text: Entire workforce satisfied with speaker’s praise?

indicators.note: What a speaker gives you is the sound of a word and not its spelling, so the next word is to be heard rather than read.

blocks.note: somebody who has eaten enough is satisfied
praise handed out is a compliment; the two spellings sound identical and only one of them means a complete set

explanation.surface: Staff who have eaten well and enjoyed the after-dinner tribute.
explanation.walkthrough: Compliment and complement are the pair of words this clue exists for — same sound, different spelling, different meaning — and only the grid decides which you write. 'Speaker' is a man at a lectern on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A full complement is the entire number of people a ship, team or office is supposed to carry, so it is the whole workforce present and correct.

clue.text: See 10
Rejected premier with expert going round north to make a pitch

indicators.note: Something rejected is thrown back, so the whole assembly is written out the other way about.
Going round a thing means enclosing it, so the letter that follows sits inside the word before it.

blocks.note: pm is the prime minister, the premier of a British government
an ace is an expert, the best there is at something
n = north on any compass

explanation.surface: A deposed prime minister touring the north with a consultant to sell something.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole assembly turns, not one piece of it, so the two chunks swap ends as well as running backwards. 'Pitch' is the trap: the football ground and the sales talk are both wrong and the tent-pegging sense is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: To encamp is to pitch camp and settle in it, so 'make a pitch' is the verb phrase read in its canvas-and-guy-ropes sense.

clue.text: Under a terrible strain, man is scathing

indicators.note: Under puts one thing below another, and below in a down entry means later.
A terrible version of a word is one that has come out wrong, its letters no longer in the order they were given.

blocks.note: six letters rearranged
a gent is a man, clipped from gentleman

explanation.surface: Somebody under pressure turning sharp-tongued with everyone around him.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as cause and effect — pressure makes people snappish — while the clue is two pieces stacked one above the other. 'Under' earns its keep in a down entry by saying which piece goes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Astringent criticism is sharp and cutting enough to sting, which is what scathing remarks do.

clue.text: Testifier calls for reduction to include page 1

indicators.note: To include something is to take it within, so what follows goes inside the word just named rather than after it.

blocks.note: a dent in your savings is a reduction in them
p = page, as printed in any index
the numeral spelt out in letters

explanation.surface: A witness insisting that any cut to the document still keeps page one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Page 1' is two instructions dressed as a page number: a one-letter abbreviation and then a numeral written out in full. 'Calls for' is joinery, easy to miss in a sentence that sounds like a demand.
explanation.definitionFit: A deponent is the person who gives evidence on oath in a deposition, which is a testifier under another name.

clue.text: Groundbreaker’s rejected last quarter’s image

indicators.note: A four-letter word divides into quarters of one letter each, and the last of those is the one thrown out.

blocks.note: a pick is the tool you break ground with

explanation.surface: A pioneer turning down the photograph used in the last three months' publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarter' offers a district or three months of trading and means a fourth of the letters instead. Four go in and three come out, and the word that goes in is a tool rather than a trailblazer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pic is the everyday shortening of picture, so it is simply an image.

clue.text: The craft of stirring kith and kin with love (not hard)

indicators.note: Stirring a mixture moves everything in it around, which is what happens to these letters.
Not, put in front of a letter's name, is the instruction to leave that letter out of the mixture.

blocks.note: kith and kin is the old phrase for friends and family, and its seven letters are the bulk of the fodder
love is a score of nothing in tennis, written as a zero
h = hard, the grade stamped on a pencil

explanation.surface: The knack of mixing family and friends together with affection and not much effort.
explanation.walkthrough: One letter is pulled out of the mixture before everything left in it is shuffled, so two instructions run at once. 'The craft of stirring' reads as a cook's skill, and craft here is a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Kon-Tiki was Thor Heyerdahl's balsa-wood raft, sailed from Peru to Polynesia in 1947, so 'the craft' names one particular vessel.

clue.text: Agreed to return one’s pet fish

indicators.note: To return something is to send it back the way it came, so those two letters are written in the opposite direction.

blocks.note: OK is what you write on a form when the thing is agreed
i is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Somebody agreeing to hand back a borrowed pet fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Two letters and then one, which is all a three-letter entry has room for, and the pair have to be read the wrong way up. The creature is the ornamental carp bred in Japan for garden ponds.
explanation.definitionFit: Koi are the big patterned carp kept in ponds and fed by hand, which makes 'pet fish' a plain description of them.

clue.text: A college matter, for the record

blocks.note: the article taken as the letter it is
c = college in the abbreviated names of institutions
to count is to matter — every vote counts

explanation.surface: A university issue being put down in the official minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matter' is a verb here and reads as a noun, which is what hides five of the seven letters in plain sight. 'For the record' is a phrase the eye slides over without noticing the definition buried in it.
explanation.definitionFit: An account is the written version of what happened, the one that goes down on paper and is referred back to.

clue.text: Plain refusal by father to take on troubles

blocks.note: no is the refusal itself
Fr is how a priest's title, Father, is written in front of his name on a church noticeboard
ills are troubles, as in the ills of the age

explanation.surface: A priest flatly declining to shoulder anybody else's problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain refusal' looks like one phrase and splits down the middle between the definition and the wordplay, which is the whole trick of the clue. Nothing marks the join.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-frills airline or hotel is stripped of everything but the basics, which is what calling something plain means.

clue.text: Officer has to revere virtually everybody? Not quite

indicators.note: Virtually a word is not quite the whole of it, so its last letter is left off.
Not quite means just short of the whole, so this word gives up its final letter too.

blocks.note: to admire is to revere
all is everybody

explanation.surface: An officer who supposedly has to look up to nearly the whole navy.
explanation.walkthrough: The same instruction is given twice in different words, once in front of its word and once behind, and each time a final letter falls away. The question mark flags the joke: this rank looks up to almost nobody.
explanation.definitionFit: An admiral is the most senior commissioned rank in a navy, so 'officer' names him by the kind of thing he is.

clue.text: Hardened, sibilant vocalist’s ‘turned into the Prince of Darkness’?

indicators.note: A sibilant is a hissing sound, so the buzzing letters in the name are written down as the hissing ones instead.

blocks.note: the nickname Ozzy Osbourne has carried since the Black Sabbath years
-fied is the ending that means made into, as in petrified or liquefied
it says the man sings, which narrows the nickname to its one famous holder

explanation.surface: A hissing singer described as having turned into heavy metal's dark lord.
explanation.walkthrough: Ozzified is the word being built — somebody turned into Ozzy — and the y softens to i before the ending, as English spelling always does. Brummie setting a clue about Birmingham's most famous export is not an accident.
explanation.definitionFit: To ossify is to turn to bone, and the past participle describes anything that has set rigid, whether a joint or an attitude.

clue.text: Stylish, small disposable pad

blocks.note: s = small, the label sewn into the collar
a nappy is the absorbent pad a baby wears, sold by the packet; an American would call it a diaper

explanation.surface: An advertisement for a neat little throwaway notepad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pad' carries the whole disguise: a writing pad in the surface, an infant's in the parse. The comma after the first word is the only sign that the sentence comes in two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Snappy means smart and well turned out — a snappy dresser is a stylish one.

clue.text: Reform’s ‘no extremist’ condition meets with dismay ultimately

indicators.note: Ultimately points at the very end of the word before it, so only that word's final letter is taken.

blocks.note: a mod is a moderate, which is precisely somebody who is no extremist
if is the little word that states a condition
the letter this word ends on

explanation.surface: A centrist policy from a political party going down badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reform' looks like the party in the news and is the definition, a plain verb. The quotation marks flag 'no extremist' as a phrase standing in for one short political label.
explanation.definitionFit: To modify a thing is to change it in parts without scrapping it, which is what the verb reform asks for.

indicators.note: A minus sign takes away whatever follows it, so the letter written after it comes out of the sum.

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for a thousand
the number written out in letters
the italicised letter named for removal

explanation.surface: A line of arithmetic claiming a thousand plus eighty, less e, comes to a grand.
explanation.walkthrough: One side of the sum really is arithmetic, because a grand is a thousand in slang. The other side is not: one number is Roman and the other has to be spelt out in words before anything can be subtracted from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand means imposing and impressive, the sense in which a mighty effort and a grand effort are the same effort.

clue.text: Leverage of drinking establishment securing Nick

blocks.note: a bar is where the drinking is done
securing a deal is gaining it
a nick in the rim of a cup is a chip out of it

explanation.surface: A pub getting hold of a man called Nick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Securing' is dressed as a container instruction and is only a synonym, which is the clue's one real piece of misdirection. The capital on Nick does the other half of the work.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargaining chip is something you hold that the other side wants, which is exactly the leverage holding it gives you.

clue.text: Smooth over Shakespeare’s unrelenting resolve?

blocks.note: to iron something is to smooth it, and to iron out a difficulty is to smooth it over
the playwright's own first name, familiar from Will Shakespeare

explanation.surface: Trying to talk the Bard out of a stubborn decision.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as a possessive and is really the setter pointing at a first name. Both halves are ordinary words, which is why an eight-letter answer arrives with no indicator anywhere in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron will is a determination nothing bends, so 'unrelenting resolve' says the same thing in other words.

clue.text: See 24
Cheese-maker’s dog food tip

indicators.note: A tip is the far end of a thing, so the letter taken is the one the word finishes on rather than the one it starts with.

blocks.note: a cur is a mongrel, a dog of no breeding
the letter this word ends on

explanation.surface: A cheesemonger passing on advice about what to feed the dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog food' looks like one item on a shopping list and is two separate instructions. 'Tip' is being used for the far end of a word rather than its first letter, the less common of its two crossword jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Curd is the solid that separates out of milk and is then pressed into cheese, so it is literally the stuff cheese is made of.

clue.text: Lowbrow entertainment – Gasp! Exclamation!

blocks.note: to pant is to gasp for breath
O is the exclamation of old verse, as in 'O for a muse of fire'

explanation.surface: A run of melodramatic noises of the sort a theatre audience makes.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash and the two exclamation marks do the disguising, so the clue reads as stage directions instead of a definition followed by two chunks. The show meant is the British Christmas one, with its dame and its booing.
explanation.definitionFit: Panto is the knockabout Christmas show British families go to — fairy tale, man in a frock, audience shouting back — which is lowbrow by design.

clue.text: Stabilising article by online pest suppressing ego

indicators.note: To suppress a thing is to hold it down inside, so the letter named goes within the word in front of it.

blocks.note: an is one of the two indefinite articles
a troll is the internet's nuisance, posting to provoke a row
the ego is the I, the self in Freud's scheme

explanation.surface: A piece written about an internet nuisance who keeps his self-regard in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suppressing' reads as a man mastering his vanity, and its real job is to bury a single letter inside another word. The answer is half of a car part's name, which is why it looks unfinished.
explanation.definitionFit: An anti-roll bar is the suspension link that stops a car leaning over in a bend, so 'stabilising' describes exactly what it does.
